Pulmonary Disorders

Community-Acquired Pneumonia, Aspiration Pneumonia, and Noninfectious Pulmonary Infiltrates

This rebuild follows the Tintinalli chapter outline rather than collapsing pneumonia into a few broad buckets. Every named heading/subheading receives narrative coverage, with the source tables and figures placed next to the topic they support.

Board trap: do not let an infiltrate plus cough end the case; classify acquisition setting, identify host risk, evaluate severity, and keep aspiration and noninfectious mimics in the differential.

COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is infection of the gas-exchanging alveolar lung that begins outside the hospital or within the early presentation window. Tintinalli emphasizes that pneumonia remains common, deadly in older adults, and expensive for health systems. The ED task is not simply to label an infiltrate, but to decide whether the acquisition setting suggests community, hospital, ventilator, or healthcare-associated pathogens.

The acquisition environment changes the antibiotic and disposition problem. A patient from home without recent healthcare exposure has a different risk profile from a dialysis patient, nursing home resident, chemotherapy patient, or recently hospitalized patient. Risk factors also identify patients more likely to aspirate, seed bacteria hematogenously, or fail outpatient care.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Pneumonia develops when organisms are inhaled, aspirated, or seeded into lung parenchyma and evade host defenses. Aspiration is common, especially when swallowing, cough, consciousness, or mucociliary clearance is impaired. Bacterial pathogens often create a stronger alveolar inflammatory response with productive cough, while atypical pathogens may cause less intense inflammation and a more subacute, nonproductive syndrome.

Inflammation fills alveoli with cells and exudate, disrupts gas exchange, and produces radiographic infiltrates. The radiographic pattern is not perfectly organism-specific, so the ED clinician combines epidemiology, host factors, vital signs, oxygenation, and imaging rather than relying on one radiographic label.

CLINICAL FEATURES

CAP often presents with cough, fever, fatigue, dyspnea, sputum production, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, hypoxia, or abnormal lung sounds. Tintinalli highlights that the pattern is not uniform: older adults, children, immunocompromised patients, and patients at extremes of age may present with altered mental status, weakness, functional decline, or minimal fever.

Classic lobar pneumonia may be dramatic, but many patients have vague or extrapulmonary complaints such as headache, nausea, diarrhea, myalgias, or rash. Clinical features should prevent both underdiagnosis in atypical presentations and overdiagnosis when noninfectious infiltrates are present.

PNEUMOCOCCAL PNEUMONIA

Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the most common identified CAP pathogen and may cause sudden fever, rigors, productive cough, pleuritic pain, and lobar infiltrate. High-risk groups include the elderly, young children, day-care exposure, HIV, sickle cell disease, and patients with underlying medical illness. Penicillin and macrolide resistance vary geographically, so local resistance patterns matter.

OTHER BACTERIAL PNEUMONIAS

Other bacterial pneumonias are shaped by host context. Staphylococcus aureus is important after viral illness, in chronic lung disease, aspiration risk, immunosuppression, nursing home exposure, and healthcare-associated settings; it can produce empyema, effusion, and abscess. Klebsiella is associated with alcoholism, diabetes, and debility. Pseudomonas risk rises with recent hospitalization, broad-spectrum antibiotics, steroids, ICU exposure, and structural lung disease. Haemophilus and Moraxella are prominent in elderly patients and chronic lung disease.

Tintinalli source

Figure 65-2

PNEUMONIA FROM ATYPICAL AGENTS

Atypical agents include Legionella, Chlamydophila, Mycoplasma, and viruses. Legionella can range from mild illness to multisystem failure with GI symptoms, hyponatremia, mental status change, and severe pneumonia. Mycoplasma often causes subacute cough, sore throat, headache, and atypical chest discomfort. Viral pneumonia can be primary or set the stage for bacterial superinfection; influenza-like illness does not exclude bacterial danger.

Tintinalli source

Figure 65-3

Pneumonia suggesting legionella.

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis begins with symptoms, signs, oxygenation, and chest imaging. Tintinalli stresses that individual symptoms and physical findings alone are not reliable enough to diagnose pneumonia. Chest radiography helps identify infiltrate, effusion, multilobar disease, cavitation, abscess, or alternative diagnoses, but immunocompromised patients can have clinical pneumonia before obvious radiographic change.

Testing should be selective. Pulse oximetry is essential. CBC and chemistry can support risk stratification, renal dosing, or detection of immunosuppression. Blood cultures and sputum studies have limited yield in uncomplicated outpatient CAP but become more relevant in severe disease, ICU admission, unusual pathogens, leukopenia, cavitary lesions, severe alcohol use, asplenia, pleural effusion, or treatment failure.

PNEUMONIA IN SPECIAL POPULATIONS

PNEUMONIA IN ALCOHOLICS

Alcohol use disorder increases pneumonia risk through aspiration, poor dentition, malnutrition, impaired cough, depressed granulocyte and lymphocyte function, and worse physiologic reserve. S. pneumoniae remains common, but Klebsiella and Haemophilus become more important, and outcomes are worse than in nonalcoholic patients.

PNEUMONIA IN DIABETICS

Diabetes independently increases pneumonia and influenza risk and worsens mortality. Diabetic patients have higher risk of S. aureus, gram-negative bacteria, mucormycosis, tuberculosis, and severe soft-tissue or bloodstream infection. Hyperglycemia and renal disease also affect disposition and antimicrobial dosing.

PNEUMONIA IN PREGNANT WOMEN

Pregnancy changes respiratory reserve and immune response. Pneumonia in pregnancy can progress quickly because oxygen consumption is higher and functional residual capacity is lower. ED care must aggressively assess oxygenation, sepsis, fetal considerations by gestational age, influenza risk, and medication safety.

PNEUMONIA IN THE ELDERLY

Elderly patients may have blunted fever, minimal cough, falls, delirium, anorexia, or functional decline rather than classic pneumonia symptoms. Comorbid disease, aspiration risk, and lower reserve increase admission risk. Disposition should not be based on x-ray alone; oxygenation, cognition, hydration, support, and ability to take medication matter.

PNEUMONIA IN NURSING HOME PATIENTS

Nursing home patients often have aspiration risk, colonization with resistant organisms, recent antibiotics, frailty, and barriers to follow-up. Tintinalli treats this as a distinct risk environment: the clinician must ask about recent hospitalization, IV antibiotics, dialysis, wound care, immunosuppression, and local resistance rather than assuming uncomplicated CAP.

PNEUMONIA IN HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS PATIENTS

HIV changes the pathogen list by CD4 count. Bacterial pneumonia may occur at higher CD4 counts, while tuberculosis, cryptococcus, histoplasmosis, and Pneumocystis become more important as CD4 falls. Pleural effusions, nodules, diffuse infiltrates, hemoptysis, and hypoxemia require broader workup than routine CAP.

PNEUMONIA IN TRANSPLANT PATIENTS

Transplant patients are shaped by immunosuppression timing. Early bacterial infections include gram-negative bacilli, S. aureus, Legionella, and fungal pathogens; later infections may involve community pathogens, opportunistic fungi, or viral disease. These patients can deteriorate with subtle findings, so lower thresholds for consultation, admission, and broad diagnostics are appropriate.

TREATMENT

Antibiotic timing and choice depend on severity, acquisition setting, comorbidities, local resistance, allergies, renal function, pregnancy, and risk for MRSA or Pseudomonas. Treatment should start promptly in ill patients, but the ED must still classify the syndrome because overtreatment and undertreatment both cause harm.

OUTPATIENT TREATMENT

Uncomplicated outpatients can often receive macrolide or doxycycline-based regimens depending on resistance and patient factors. Comorbid patients need broader coverage, commonly a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone when appropriate. Rosen's newer CAP table narrows macrolide monotherapy and aligns with modern resistance concerns.

INPATIENT TREATMENT

Non-ICU inpatients require coverage for typical and atypical pathogens. ICU patients, HCAP-risk patients, and those with Pseudomonas or MRSA risk need broader empiric regimens. Avoid monotherapy that fails to cover atypicals when they matter, and adjust dosing for renal insufficiency and local antibiograms.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Most CAP patients do not need hospitalization, but disposition is not a vibes-based decision. PSI, CURB-65/CRB-65, and Rosen severe-CAP/SMART-COP tools support decisions, while clinical judgment remains necessary for younger patients, social instability, severe hypoxemia, immunocompromise, or rapidly changing physiology.

Admit patients with sepsis, need for mechanical ventilation, shock, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, hypoxemia, inability to take oral therapy, poor follow-up, or high-risk comorbidities. Discharged patients need explicit return precautions, completion of therapy, hydration, reassessment if worsening, and prevention counseling including pneumococcal and influenza vaccination when appropriate.

ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Aspiration pneumonia is infection after inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric material. Aspiration alone does not equal pneumonia; infection develops when aspirated material, bacterial burden, host physiology, and lung defense failure overlap. It is common in nursing home patients and patients with altered consciousness, neurologic disease, dysphagia, poor oral hygiene, or tube feeds.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Aspirated volume, pH, bacterial flora, and host defenses determine whether the patient develops chemical pneumonitis, bacterial pneumonia, airway obstruction, or chronic aspiration syndrome. Oral hygiene and dental disease increase bacterial load. Large-volume aspiration can cause rapid hypoxia, bronchospasm, and low-grade fever within hours.

Tintinalli source

Table 65-13

Risk factors for aspiration.

Tintinalli source

Table 65-14

Aspiration syndromes.

CLINICAL FEATURES AND TREATMENT

Aspiration pneumonitis tends to develop quickly after a witnessed event and may improve over 24 to 48 hours. Aspiration pneumonia may be delayed, unwitnessed, and associated with cough, dyspnea, fever, tachypnea, and dependent infiltrates. Treat community-acquired aspiration pneumonia with CAP-active antibiotics when infection is likely; add anaerobic emphasis when abscess, empyema, severe periodontal disease, or necrotizing infection is suspected.

DISPOSITION

Healthy patients who aspirate a small amount of nontoxic material may be observed briefly and discharged if symptoms resolve. Admit patients with persistent hypoxia, respiratory distress, sepsis, inability to protect the airway, significant comorbidity, or aspiration pneumonia requiring antibiotics and monitoring.

NONINFECTIOUS PULMONARY INFILTRATES

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Noninfectious infiltrates are radiographic abnormalities not caused by infection. They are important because they can mimic pneumonia and may be falsely treated with repeated antibiotics. Consider noninfectious mimics when the story is atypical, cultures are negative, infiltrates persist, or symptoms fail to improve.

Tintinalli source

Table 65-15

Noninfectious causes of pulmonary infiltrates.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Dyspnea is the dominant symptom, but cough, fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, wheezing, fatigue, and hypoxemia may occur. The differential includes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, eosinophilic lung disease, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, organizing pneumonia, vasculitis, drug-induced pneumonitis, chemical pneumonitis, radiation pneumonitis, malignancy, leukemic infiltrates, fat emboli, alveolar hemorrhage, and ARDS.

TREATMENT

Treatment is directed at the underlying cause after stabilizing oxygenation and ventilation. Some entities require corticosteroids or immunosuppression, some require removal of an offending drug or exposure, and some require ventilatory support. The ED role is to avoid anchoring on infection while still treating sepsis or hypoxemia when present.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Hospitalize patients with hypoxemia, hypercapnia, increased work of breathing, hemoptysis, unstable vital signs, or uncertain diagnosis requiring urgent evaluation. Stable patients with mild symptoms may need pulmonary or specialty follow-up, but only after dangerous mimics and oxygenation problems are addressed.
